extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, filmmakers, and storytellers (film students and professional writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on designing scene tempo/pace, narrative progressions, transitions, and the Crisis–Climax–Resolution portion of a screenplay or film story. Teaches how to structure and pace scenes to produce powerful climaxes and meaningful endings.

rubrics_metrics.name: French scenes / scene subdivision
rubrics_metrics.description: Within a single location, the entrance or exit of principal characters or shifts in sublocation creates a new scene (a 'French Scene').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sublocations inside a set to create many small scenes (e.g., drinking fountain, cloakroom, one end of the table versus the other). Examples: TWELVE ANGRY MEN—over eighty French Scenes create rhythm. Staging French Scenes builds exciting rhythm by cutting between different groupings and single characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tempo
rubrics_metrics.description: Tempo is the level of activity within a scene via dialogue, action, or a combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: lovers whispering = low tempo; courtroom argument or riot = high tempo; a character staring out a window making a decision = low tempo. Tempo interacts with scene length to produce pace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progression of scenes to accelerate pace
rubrics_metrics.description: In a well-told story, progression of scenes and sequences should accelerate pace as you head toward act climaxes: scenes progressively shorten while activity becomes brisker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorten scene lengths and raise tempo to hurl audience toward act climaxes. However, major reversal scenes (climaxes) are often long, slow, and tense — they should 'breathe' and be allowed to retard pace at the climactic moment. Balance telescoping rhythm with a spiraling tempo so the big pause at the Climax is earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earn the pause / Law of diminishing returns
rubrics_metrics.description: You must 'earn the pause' — if you pause too often or precede the Climax with long sluggish scenes, the Climax will fall flat (Law of Diminishing Returns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid lengthening and slowing scenes prior to a major reversal. Instead telescope rhythm and increase tempo toward the Climax so that when you slow, the pause remains effective. Clichés exist because the technique works, but ignorance of the principle cripples the Climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pace begins in the screenplay; control rhythm and tempo
rubrics_metrics.description: Pace and rhythm must be set by the screenwriter in the screenplay; cinema is kinetic and the screenplay should prepare the way for filmmakers and editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the screenplay doesn't shape progressions and tempo, the editor will—and may cut favorite moments. Screenwriters must master film aesthetics rather than treating scripts like novel drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressing progression (overall principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine story progression calls upon increasing human capacity, willpower, change in characters' lives, and jeopardy; there are four primary techniques to express this progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The four techniques are (1) social progression, (2) personal progression, (3) symbolic ascension, and (4) ironic ascension. Use one or combine them to make the story sense of escalation clear to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Widen the impact of character actions into society: start intimately, then let actions ramify outward to touch more people and escalate stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spread the effect gradually through progressions. This explains why protagonists are often in positions (lawyers, doctors, politicians, etc.) that allow private events to expand into social consequence. Examples: LONE STAR, MEN IN BLACK.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Drive actions deeply into intimate relationships and the inner lives of characters: if you cannot go wide, go deep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with a solvable personal conflict, then hammer downward emotionally/psychologically/morally to dark secrets and unspoken truths. Example: ORDINARY PEOPLE descends from family tension to grievous pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic ascension / symbolic progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Build the symbolic charge of the story’s imagery from the particular to the universal—images accumulate greater meaning as the story progresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slip symbolism quietly and gradually so it operates subliminally. Choose images that gather meaning until characters, settings, and events stand for universal ideas. Examples: THE DEER HUNTER (factory worker → warrior → 'The Hunter'), THE TERMINATOR (city as labyrinth). Tie to a Controlling Idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ironic ascension / ironic progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn progression on irony—play the discrepancy between appearance and reality or actions and results to generate story energy and pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony must be subtly implied, not labeled. The text gives six ironic story patterns (e.g., he gets what he wanted too late; he throws away what later is indispensable; to reach a goal he takes steps that lead away). Use precise setups of expectation and reversal to create ironic progression (examples: OTHELLO, TOOTSIE, BRINGING UP BABY).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of transition
rubrics_metrics.description: Between two scenes you need a linking third element—the hinge—that joins the tail of Scene A with the head of Scene B, found in what the scenes have in common or in opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common/opposition hinge types include: characterization trait (cut from bratty child to childish adult), an action (foreplay → afterglow or chatter → cold silence), an object (greenhouse → woodland), a word (repeated phrase), quality of light (dawn shadows → sunset shade), a sound (waves → breathing), or an idea (birth → overture). Avoid lazy transition clichés by imaginatively finding a link.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis is decision—the ultimate, story-defining decision when the protagonist has exhausted actions and faces a last, no-tomorrow choice (Chinese ideogram: Danger/Opportunity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Crisis is the Obligatory Scene anticipated from the Inciting Incident onward. It must be a true dilemma (irreconcilable goods, lesser of two evils, or two simultaneous goods/evils) and reveals deep character and the story's primary value. The moment is one of maximal tension and willpower.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis must be a true dilemma and reveal primary value
rubrics_metrics.description: The Crisis must present an authentic dilemma—a choice between irreconcilable goods or evils—and how the protagonist chooses reveals the story's primary value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the central value has been ambiguous, the Crisis decision brings it to the fore. The scene provides the most penetrating view of the protagonist's humanity and must be allowed to 'freeze' as tension builds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis as Obligatory Scene: on-screen, static, and unskinned
rubrics_metrics.description: The Crisis decision must be shown on-screen, deliberately static, and not skimmed over or put offscreen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not cut away or treat the Crisis as incidental; the audience wants to suffer through the agonizing choice with the protagonist. Examples: THELMA & LOUISE (hesitation over 'go')—build tension by delaying and freezing the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis placement depends on climactic action length
rubrics_metrics.description: The location/timing of the Crisis is determined by the length of the climactic action; generally Crisis and Climax occur in the last minutes in the same scene, but variations exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some stories use a Crisis that immediately leads to a short Climax (THELMA & LOUISE). Others use a Crisis that triggers an expansive climactic action filling the final act (CASABLANCA). Rarely, the Crisis may follow the Inciting Incident and the entire story becomes climactic action (e.g., many James Bond films). Be aware of risks: early Crisis can lead to repetitiveness and variety problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis within the Climax / Turning Point within Climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Embedding additional gaps between expectation and result inside the climactic action—a Turning Point within the Climax—creates especially majestic and memorable endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Split probability from necessity one more time during the climactic action to generate deep insight. Examples: STAR WARS (single decisive choice guided by the Force) vs. THE EMPIRE STRIKES BACK (multiple gaps and decisions as revelations explode).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of Crisis and Climax across locations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Crisis may occur in one location with the Climax later in another; when this happens, splice them tightly in filmic time and space to avoid draining energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cut from Crisis to unrelated material (e.g., a subplot), you risk anticlimax. If Crisis and Climax are separated, fuse them by cutting so the audience perceives continuity. Example: KRAMER VS. KRAMER—Crisis is a courtroom decision; Climax is the walk in Central Park.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climax (definition and purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Story Climax is the crowning Major Reversal—a revolution in values (positive to negative or vice versa) with maximum charge, absolute and irreversible, that produces meaning and thus emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Climactic action must be 'pure, clear, and self-evident' requiring no explanatory dialogue. It can be catastrophically large or outwardly trivial depending on context. The Climax should fulfill anticipation and deliver the promised emotion, often with an unexpected insight (Turning Point).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning produces emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Climax must produce meaning (a value swing) because meaning is what creates emotional payoff in the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not spectacle, stars, effects, or money—meaning is the core. Design the climactic action to produce a clear value reversal tied to the story's Controlling Idea so the audience feels emotional satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work backward from the Climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the Climax is conceived, rewrite backward: supply the hows and whys so every scene thematically or structurally supports the ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All scenes must be justified in light of the Climax. If a scene can be cut without disturbing the impact of the ending, it must be cut. Climax-first thinking often rewrites the story in reverse to ensure inevitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key Image / Spectacle and Truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a Key Image within the climactic action that sums up and concentrates all meaning and emotion—combining spectacle (visual power) and truth (Controlling Idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Key Image acts as a coda: one memorable image that, when recalled, brings the whole film back. Truffaut's 'Spectacle and Truth' means a climax written for the eye and grounded in the story's controlling idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inevitable and unexpected ending (Aristotle)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ending must be both inevitable (in hindsight the only possible outcome) and unexpected (the way it happens must surprise the audience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given the characters and world as presented, the Climax should feel unavoidable yet deliver insight or method the audience did not anticipate. Combine inevitability with a withheld Turning Point inside the Climax for maximum effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give the audience the promised emotion, but not how they expect
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer determines which emotion (up-ending, down-ending, irony) is promised by the way the story is told and must deliver it, though not in the obvious manner the audience expects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't betray the audience's promised trajectory. People don't always require happy endings—what they require is emotional satisfaction. Use unexpected means (Turning Points) to fulfill the promised emotion. Examples: THE GODFATHER PART II, THE ENGLISH PATIENT, DANGEROUS LIAISONS show that down-endings can still be commercially and emotionally satisfying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climax should resolve subplots effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: If possible, climax remaining subplots within the Central Plot's Climax so one final action by the protagonist settles multiple threads; if impossible, climax subplots earlier in descending importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A multiplying, consolidating Climax (e.g., Rick putting Ilsa and Laszlo on the plane in CASABLANCA) is powerful. If you cannot consolidate, order subplot climaxes from least to most important to build overall momentum toward the Central Plot's Climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid transition clichés but find imaginative links
rubrics_metrics.description: Although transition clichés abound after a century of filmmaking, imaginative study will find a link between almost any two scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rely on stock bridges; deliberately search for a creative hinge (common or opposite) to maintain thematic and tonal continuity through cuts.
